messages.subject: plotting issues
parts:
Hello everyone, 
I have got some issues concerning the plot of the tree with ranges after running an analysis based on the GeoSSE model + temporal stratified. It seems that the ancestral and tip ranges are not correctly indicated (as seen in the attached tree) through the terminals that have the opposite trait, says, 0. Is there any solution? Has somebody got a similar error?
My best regards,
José Ricardo.

messages.author: 115d05260b0c341a
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] plotting issues
parts:
Hi -- this looks like it might be an issue with whether or not the null range is included in the model, vs. in the plot?  Search your script on include_null_range and make sure it matches throughout.

PS I wouldn't call it a GeoSSE model, DIVALIKE (and the other BioGeoBEARS models) can be viewed as special cases of ClaSSE models, but with lineage extinction ("E") set to 0, the birthrate (speciation=S) fixed to the Yule (pure-birth process), and with state-dependent speciation (SS) only existing in the limited sense that different kinds of cladogenesis get different weights.  See: 

Matzke, Nicholas J. (2022). Statistical comparison of DEC and DEC+J is identical to comparison of two ClaSSE submodels, and is therefore valid. Journal of Biogeography, 49(10), 1805-1824. doi: 10.1111/jbi.14346 

Cheers,
Nick

Dear Nick,
thank you for your answer. Unfortunately, I have included the null range both in the model and in the plot, as you can see in the part of my attached script.

SCRIPT (part):
#######################################################
# DIVALIKEj + t12+t21+m2+x: Distance-dependent: changing distance
#######################################################
BioGeoBEARS_run_object = define_BioGeoBEARS_run()
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$print_optim = TRUE
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$calc_ancprobs=TRUE        # get ancestral states from optim run
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$max_range_size = max_range_size
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$num_cores_to_use = num_cores
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$use_optimx=TRUE
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$speedup=TRUE
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$geogfn = geog_values
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$trfn = trfn
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$timesfn = timeSeries
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$distsfn = distSeries
BioGeoBEARS_run_object = readfiles_BioGeoBEARS_run(BioGeoBEARS_run_object)
BioGeoBEARS_run_object = section_the_tree(inputs=BioGeoBEARS_run_object, make_master_table=TRUE, plot_pieces=FALSE, cut_fossils = FALSE)
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$return_condlikes_table = TRUE
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$calc_TTL_loglike_from_condlikes_table = TRUE
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$calc_ancprobs = TRUE
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$on_NaN_error = -1000000

# time-stratify to break up long branches if you see major differences in lnL
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$useAmbiguities = TRUE

#######################################################

# interpretation of DIVA, constructed by modelling DIVA's
# processes the way DEC does, but only allowing the
# processes DIVA allows (widespread vicariance: yes; subset
# sympatry: no; see Ronquist & Sanmartin 2011, Figure 4).

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$include_null_range = TRUE

# plot:
#######################################################
# Plot ancestral states
#######################################################
# Setup
results_object = res_t12_t21_m2_changingDistance_divaLikej
scriptdir = np(system.file("extdata/a_scripts", package="BioGeoBEARS"))
wd = np('D:/Dropbox/papers_books/relógio/biogeo_belos/results/material')
setwd(wd)

# Double-check your working directory with getwd()
getwd()


# unlockBinding("last.warning", baseenv())

## specify the tree file
# trfn <- "example_data/bombacoideae_phylogeny.newick"
trfn <- 'tBelos_totalEvid_SA.newick'

max_range_size = 4
num_cores = 8

pdffn = "plebe_DIVALIKE+J_M7_v2.pdf"
pdf(pdffn, paper = 'a4r')

analysis_titletxt ="DIVALIKE+j on plebejum group (model 7)"

# Look at your phylogeny:
tr = read.tree(trfn)
geog_values <- "nepoidea_areaClassification_bioregions.txt" # distribuição do grupo estudado
tipranges = getranges_from_LagrangePHYLIP(lgdata_fn = geog_values)

# States
res1 = plot_BioGeoBEARS_results(results_object, analysis_titletxt, addl_params=list("j"),
        plotwhat="text", label.offset=2, tipcex=0.7, statecex=0.7, splitcex=0.6,
        titlecex=0.5, plotsplits=TRUE, cornercoords_loc=scriptdir, include_null_range=TRUE
        tr=tr, tipranges=tipranges)

# Pie chart
plot_BioGeoBEARS_results(results_object, analysis_titletxt, addl_params=list("j"),
  plotwhat="pie", label.offset=2, tipcex=0.7, statecex=0.7, splitcex=0.6, titlecex=0.5,
  plotsplits=TRUE, cornercoords_loc=scriptdir, include_null_range=TRUE, tr=tr, tipranges=tipranges)

dev.off()
##############################################################

As I have used a discrete morphological trait in order to evaluate whether the dispersal ability depends on that evolving trait, It seems that the ancestral and tip ranges of those taxa with the condition "0" were not correctly indicated (as seen in the attached tree). You see?


 In addition, I have another question:

my dataset size is small (about 39 terminals), and the best model was a DIVALIKE trait-dependent model + changing distance over time. Given that it was impossible to simulate models with the possibility of changing the distance over time, I decided to simulate DIVALIKE trait-dependent models with m1 = 1 and m2 = 0.5 (which was the actual value of my m2 parameter) without changing the distance over time (without a stratified time matrix and its respective distance matrix for each epoch). My DIVALIKE model with those conditions is not, however, the best model (i.e., without change in the distance over time). Therefore, DIVALIKE with m2 = 1 or DIVALIKE m2 = 0.5 is the same since LRT is nonsignificant. So, how dare I be if I check the rate of true positive results with my simulations? What am I supposed to expect, given that both models (i.e., DIVALIKE with m2 = 1 and DIVALIKE with m2 = 0.5) are the same? A positive rate equals the P-value cutoff as the dataset size increase?

My apologies for many questions.

My best regards,

As I have used a discrete morphological trait in order to evaluate whether the dispersal ability depends on that evolving trait, It seems that the ancestral and tip ranges of those taxa with the condition "0" were not correctly indicated (as seen in the attached tree). You see?

If you are doing a trait-dependent dispersal model, your ancestral state estimates after the ML run are the probabilities of the JOINT geography+trait states, at each node.  

To get this plotted correctly, you then have to collapse the joint geog+trait ancestral state estimates into a:

(a) a geography-only ancestral state estimates results object
(b) a traits-only ancestral state estimates results object

Now (a) can be plotted like normal biogeography, and (b) can be plotted by setting include_null_range to FALSE and max_range_size to 1.


A complete example is available in the zipfile at:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biosci-395-labs

Here is the code for extracting geog-only and trait-only ancestral states, from the joint ancestral states:

==============
#######################################################
# Extract just geography ancestral states from geog+trait ancestral states
#######################################################
geog_res = get_geog_from_traitgeog_results(res=resDECj_t12_t21_m2, num_trait_states=2)

#######################################################
# Extract just trait ancestral states from geog+trait ancestral states
#######################################################
trait_res = get_trait_from_traitgeog_results(res=resDECj_t12_t21_m2, num_trait_states=2)
tipranges = getranges_from_LagrangePHYLIP(lgdata_fn=slashslash(paste(labpt2a, "geog.data", sep="/")))

#######################################################
# Plot the geographic ancestral states
#######################################################
analysis_titletxt = "S. conifers: Geog reconstruction under DEC+J+trait"

results_object = geog_res
res2 = plot_BioGeoBEARS_results(results_object, analysis_titletxt, addl_params=list("j"), plotwhat="text", label.offset=0.45, tipcex=0.7, statecex=0.7, splitcex=0.6, titlecex=0.8, plotsplits=TRUE, cornercoords_loc=scriptdir, include_null_range=TRUE, tr=tr, tipranges=tipranges)

# Pie chart
# plot_BioGeoBEARS_results(results_object, analysis_titletxt, addl_params=list("j"), plotwhat="pie", label.offset=0.45, tipcex=0.7, statecex=0.7, splitcex=0.6, titlecex=0.8, plotsplits=TRUE, cornercoords_loc=scriptdir, include_null_range=TRUE, tr=tr, tipranges=tipranges)


#######################################################
# Plot the trait ancestral states
#######################################################
analysis_titletxt = "S. conifers: Trait reconstruction under DEC+J+trait"
results_object = trait_res
res2 = plot_BioGeoBEARS_results(results_object, analysis_titletxt, addl_params=list("t12","t21"), plotwhat="text", label.offset=0.45, tipcex=0.7, statecex=0.7, splitcex=0.6, titlecex=0.8, plotsplits=TRUE, cornercoords_loc=scriptdir, include_null_range=FALSE, tr=tr, tipranges=trait_values)
==============

In addition, I have another question:

my dataset size is small (about 39 terminals), and the best model was a DIVALIKE trait-dependent model + changing distance over time. Given that it was impossible to simulate models with the possibility of changing the distance over time, I decided to simulate DIVALIKE trait-dependent models with m1 = 1 and m2 = 0.5 (which was the actual value of my m2 parameter) without changing the distance over time (without a stratified time matrix and its respective distance matrix for each epoch). My DIVALIKE model with those conditions is not, however, the best model (i.e., without change in the distance over time). Therefore, DIVALIKE with m2 = 1 or DIVALIKE m2 = 0.5 is the same since LRT is nonsignificant. So, how dare I be if I check the rate of true positive results with my simulations? What am I supposed to expect, given that both models (i.e., DIVALIKE with m2 = 1 and DIVALIKE with m2 = 0.5) are the same? A positive rate equals the P-value cutoff as the dataset size increase?

My guess is that, for 39 tips, it will be hard to detect* an effect size of m2=0.5.  In our recent papers with the trait-dependent dispersal model, it looked roughly like this in simulation-inference tests (from memory):

Effect size of m2=0.5 -- needs 150+ tips
Effect size of m2=0.125 -- needs ~50 tips
Effect size of m2=0.0 -- needs ~25 tips

This should not be surprising: stronger effects are easier to detect. 

(* detect means e.g.: get a p-value <0.05 in a LRT)

Now, there is nothing magical about a p<0.05 cutoff.  You could, say, get an m2 estimate of 0.51, the LRT p-value is 0.2, and you could report that and say it's evidence for the hypothesis that the trait matters for dispersal; it's just that it is very weak evidence.  Basically the LRT is telling you that, if the null model (m2=1.0) is true, you would get an m2 estimate of 0.51 or less 20% of the time.

So, to a first approximation, the LRT p-value cutoff does not change with dataset size.  (There is probably more that could be said there, the argument for the LRT operation is an "in the limit of large data" argument, so it might be too generous with small dataset size; but it would be in the details, and anyway, adjustments would make it harder to get a statistically-significant result. 

(Anecdotally, in the various simulation-inference experiments I have done, I haven't noticed any particular bias in the LRT with dataset size; these are when simulating under the actual null model and then fitting an alternative model.  A stronger argument would be that the real-life process that produced real data is always going to be much more complex than the alternative model, and that any deviation between real-life and the null model might be picked up as evidence against the null & thus interpreted as in favor of the alternative.  This (a) again means that the LRT is, if anything, being generous, so corrections would make it harder to claim statistical significance, and (b) gets us into the general philosophy of hypothesis-testing in a world where "all models are wrong". The short version is this leads me to favour AICc over LRT (although I typically do both), try to compare a bunch of models at once with AICc (6-50ish), and always acknowledge that the AICc-best model is relatively the best, but with no expectation that it is the true model, and that some future model that we haven't thought-of/programmed yet could always be a better fit.)

Cheers,
Nick
